Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, the trigger pattern is difficult to reconcile clinically: explosion/bang sounds and hospital/antiseptic smells imply very different trauma contexts or aftermaths, with no accompanying memory or appraisal content linking them into a coherent assault narrative. This is more than merely unusual because the trigger set suggests mixed trauma cues rather than one assault profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' does not fit well with the rest of the profile. Threat items focus on immediate environmental danger and startle, while memory items center on grief, auditory recall, and emotional numbing; none support a prominent bodily injury theme. In the absence of corroborating assault-related injury cues, this appraisal appears mismatched.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: Given the very strong Triggers → Threat edge, trigger items should plausibly feed the specific threat pattern. 'Being naked' can fit vulnerability and danger, but explosion sounds and hospital smells do not connect well to the selected threat items for a single assault formulation, making the trigger-to-threat linkage clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, hospital/antiseptic smell is only coherent if the assault involved serious injury or hospital treatment, but nothing in threat, memory, or appraisals anchors the trauma to a medical context. In this profile it stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of the formulation.

'Being naked' as a trigger implies a sexual assault, humiliation, medical exposure, or a very specific vulnerability context. The other items do not support that context: threat items reflect generalized hypervigilance/startle, memory items do not indicate bodily violation or exposure, and appraisals focus on self-blame/protection of others rather than sexualized shame. This makes the trigger hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

For an assault trauma, 'being naked' as a trigger is not impossible, but without any corroborating memory, threat, or appraisal content suggesting sexual assault, humiliation, or clothing-related vulnerability, it stands out as poorly integrated with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items point to alcohol cues and loss of control, while threat items center on hypervigilance/startle; this specific trigger appears disconnected from the described trauma representation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed
issues.explanation: 'I should have protected others and I failed' implies the patient experienced the assault in a protector/caretaker role or alongside endangered others. No memory, trigger, or threat item references other people being harmed or the patient's responsibility toward them. The rest of the appraisals are self-focused incompetence/blame, so this item is the main cross-node inconsistency.

vignette: Sixteen years ago, in the dimly lit basement office of a community center, Marcus, an African American principal, found himself pinned against a metal filing cabinet. The man who cornered him reeked of sour whiskey and stale tobacco. Before Marcus could step back, heavy hands wrenched his arms behind his back, forcing his face into the carpet. "Do as I say," the man had growled, his grip unyielding. Marcus tried to speak, to reason, but the pressure on his shoulders only tightened, stripping him of any leverage. He remembered the cold linoleum against his cheek, the terrible sensation of his body being moved against his will, and the quiet conviction that his own attempt to de-escalate the situation had been his only mistake. The man forced him to lie still, counting the seconds until the door clicked shut and the footsteps faded. When Marcus returned to his duties, the architecture of his days shifted. He began tracing the perimeter of every room he entered, his eyes immediately locking onto the door, the stairwell, the fire exit. He told his wife, Eleanor, that it was merely a practical habit, but what frightened him most was the steady certainty that the next time, there would be no escape. During a faculty luncheon in the staff lounge, a teacher celebrated a retirement by uncorking a bottle of amber liqueur. The moment the paper seal broke and the sharp, sweet smell of alcohol drifted across the table, Marcus's chair scraped back against the tile. His pulse hammered. He was certain the room would tilt, that he would be overpowered again if he stayed still. He left without explanation, the taste of copper in his mouth. At home, memories arrived as separate, heavy presences. Sometimes the recollection would surface unbidden in the grocery store or while watering the garden, and a wave of crushing sorrow would lock his breath. Other times, the memory would arrive completely stripped of feeling. He would sit on the edge of his bed and narrate the event to himself in a flat, distant tone, watching the words detach from his own life. He had come to believe he could no longer rely on himself. Every time he hesitated before signing a permission slip, every time he second-guessed a decision in a boardroom, that conviction deepened. He stopped calling his former colleagues for advice. He could not rely on anyone else to keep him safe, just as he could not rely on himself. The event had happened because he had misread the situation, because he had failed to keep his distance. Weeks turned into months. He avoided late-night school functions, chose routes to work that bypassed dimly lit parking garages, and sat with his back to the wall in every restaurant. His wife noticed how he flinched when she reached for his shoulder without warning, how he jumped when the kettle whistled or a car door slammed down the street. At the same time, the memory of that basement office would crackle in his skull, the crackle of a voice and the heavy thud of boots echoing exactly as they had. He stopped attending staff parties, declined invitations from friends, and gradually withdrew from the community he had spent decades building. These shifts in his routine existed alongside the widening space between him and the life he once knew. Now at seventy-seven, Marcus sits in his study, the morning light catching the dust on his diplomas. Eleanor has left him a cup of tea on the desk, but he barely notices the steam. What finally brought him here was a staff meeting last week where a young teacher leaned over his desk to hand him a folder. The sudden movement made him gasp and swipe his hand across the wood, sending the papers scattering. He saw his own face in her eyes-pale, startled, unrecognizable. He had spent a lifetime teaching boys and girls how to navigate a dangerous world, but he no longer knew how to navigate his own mind. He is hoping to find a way to stop the waiting, to quiet the echoes, to trust that he can once again stand in a room without bracing for the next strike. He fears the day he can no longer remember who he is when the silence finally comes.
